title: The Ensoniq ES5505 OTIS registers
covers: the sixteen register addresses of the Ensoniq ES5505 OTIS sound device, whose meaning the page register selects, as its specification describes them and as MAME's device handles them

rows.text: The registers of a voice are reached by the A3-A0 address lines, the page register directing the data flow to a particular voice.
The abbreviation in parentheses after a register's name may be used interchangeably.
Every bit of the voice specific registers can be written to.
Every bit of the voice specific registers can also be read back from the register.
Register 0 is the Control Register, an eight bit register that directs various aspects of the chip.
LP4 and LP3, lowpass pole 4 and lowpass pole 3, select one of four filter configurations.
With LP4 and LP3 both 0, filter poles 4 and 3 are high pass with K2.
With LP4 0 and LP3 1 pole 3 is low pass with K1; with 1 0 both poles are low pass with K2.
With LP4 1 and LP3 1 pole 4 is low pass with K2 and pole 3 is low pass with K1.
Filter poles one and two are low pass and use K1.
CA1 and CA0 are a two bit code assigning the voice to one of four serial output channels.
Channel 0 is also connected to the pulse width modulated playback outputs.
IRQ is a status flag showing the voice requested service through the interrupt vector or has a request pending.
DIR is the direction the sample is scanned: zero increments through memory, one decrements, and bidirectional looping toggles it at the loop start or end.
IRQE enables the voice's interrupt when it is one.
Bidirectional looping is enabled if BLE and LPE are both one.
LPE enables looping; with LPE zero the accumulator stops at the loop stop, the start and stop roles reverse when DIR is one, and BLE is ignored.
BS is output on the BS pin at the same time as the address of a memory cycle, for choosing between two 1Mword banks.
STOPI stops the address ALU from changing the voice during processing, so the processor may change the control register or the accumulator.
STOPO does the same and is set when looping is disabled and the accumulator reaches the loop stop; both STOPI and STOPO must be zero for the voice to run.
The Frequency Control register defines the rate the address ALU steps through the sample memory.
The frequency word is fifteen bits, left justified, six bits of integer and nine of fraction.
Pages 32 through 63 address six sixteen bit filter storage registers in each voice, for testing and initialization.
Register 1 of those pages is sixteen bits and holds the last output of the filter's final stage, the data presented to the converter.
Pages 64 through 128 address eight output channel registers, a mode register and the pot A/D register, reached when the page register's MSB is one.
Channel 0's left and right registers hold the left and right volume multiplications and feed serial port 0 and the PWM D/A output.
These registers can be written when the serial mode register's TEST bit is set.
These registers can not be read.
A write to channel 0's pair does nothing: its case falls through the other channel labels to a bare break.
MAME forces the control word's top four bits to one, whatever the write carried, and the read returns them set.
MAME's high block handles register 0x00 as the same Control Register of the voice.
Registers 2 and 3 hold the 24 bit loop start: register 2 its upper 13 bits and register 3 its lower 11.
The loop start's upper thirteen bits are right justified.
The loop start's lower eleven bits are left justified.
The loop start is where the accumulator jumps when it reaches the loop end, and holds a 20 bit integer part and a 4 bit fractional nibble.
Register 2 of pages 32 to 63 holds the last output of the filter's third stage, which feeds the fourth stage.
That register is sixteen bits wide.
Register 3 of those pages records the third stage's output of the previous sample time, which the high pass mode of pole 4 needs.
That register is sixteen bits wide as well.
Channel 1's left and right registers do what channel 0's do, without the PWM outputs, and feed serial port 1.
They can be accessed for testing in the same way as channel 0's registers.
A write to channel 1's pair does nothing: its case falls through the other channel labels to a bare break.
Registers 4 and 5 hold the loop end, partitioned as the start: a right justified 13 bit MSW and a left justified 11 bit LSW.
The loop end's upper thirteen bits are right justified.
The loop end's lower eleven bits are left justified.
The loop end marks the end of a loop in the sample memory, and the start and end registers reverse their roles when the direction bit is one.
The end register has the start register's integer and fractional partition.
Register 4 of pages 32 to 63 holds the last output of the filter's second stage, which feeds the third.
That register is sixteen bits wide.
Register 5 records the second stage's output of the previous sample time, which the high pass mode of pole 3 needs.
That register is sixteen bits wide as well.
Channel 2's left and right registers are the same as channel 1's, connected to serial port 2.
They are accessed for testing as the channel 1 registers are.
A write to channel 2's pair does nothing: its case falls through the other channel labels to a bare break.
The filter cutoff high register sets the 3 dB point of poles three and four, and its use is discussed with the digital filter.
It is a twelve bit register, left justified, using bits 15 through 4.
The filter cutoff low register sets the 3 dB point of poles one and two, and its use is discussed with the digital filter.
It is a twelve bit register, left justified, using bits 15 through 4.
Register 6 of pages 32 to 63 holds the last output of the filter's first stage, which feeds the second.
That register is sixteen bits wide.
Channel 3's registers serve serial port 3, which the A/D bit turns into a serial input.
The received data is held for the processor, and the two registers are readable in any mode.
They can only be written for testing, as the earlier channel registers can.
A write to channel 3's pair does nothing: its case falls through the other channel labels to a bare break.
The left volume register is an eight bit register that holds the left channel's amplitude as a four bit mantissa and a four bit exponent.
The eight bits are left justified in the register's word.
The filter output is multiplied by a five bit value, a leading one and the four mantissa bits, and the product is shifted by the exponent.
The right volume register defines the right channel's amplitude, with the same contents as the left, and the two pan the signal.
The right volume register's eight bits are left justified as the left register's are.
The accumulator is a 29 bit register divided into an accumulator high part and an accumulator low part.
The twenty integer bits address the sample memory and the nine fractional bits give the frequency resolution and the interpolation.
The accumulator's high half holds its 13 bits right justified.
The accumulator's low half is a full 16 bit word.
The accumulator also holds the waveform start position, which is not the loop start position.
The serial mode register holds the bits that configure and test the serial and PWM output ports.
A write to the serial mode register stores the bits that configure and test the serial and PWM ports.
The five MSB bits are the channel registers' guard bits, which test their overflow detection.
SONY/BB selects whether serial input on port 3 follows the Sony or the Burr-Brown convention.
TEST turns off the signal accumulation and allows write access to the channel registers; A/D puts serial port 3 in input mode and is set on chip reset.
When a channel register is written, the five guard bits are written to its five most significant bits.
The pot A/D register holds the digital count of the conversion for tracking pots and wheels, compared against an internal reference of about 2.8 V.
The counter's value is loaded into the register for reading by the processor.
MAME keeps SONY/BB, TEST and A/D in bits 0x0001 to 0x0004 of the mode word, and forces bits 0x07F8 to one.
A write to the channel registers does nothing: the eight cases hold only a break.
A write to register 0x0C does nothing in the voice and filter page blocks: their cases hold only a break.
A read of the pot register returns the board callback's value with its low six bits cleared when one is installed, and zero otherwise; the device does no conversion.
The Active Voice Register defines how many voices are enabled to produce sound.
The register uses bits 4 through 0, encoding values 31 through 0.
The active voice count is the register's value plus one, and it sets the output sample rate: 19.5 kHz with all 32 voices, 39 kHz with 16.
The Voice Interrupt Vector register tells the microprocessor which voice caused an interrupt.
The processor reads this register for the voice number in bits 4 through 0; bit 7 monitors the IRQ output line, which goes high after the read.
The Page register reaches the set of 16 registers that control a voice; it appears at location F in all pages.
128 pages are accessed through the page register.
Locations 0 through A of pages 0 to 31 hold a voice's most used settings.
Locations 1 through 6 of pages 32 to 63 reach the filter's temporary registers, and locations 0 through 8 of pages 64 to 127 the serial and special mode registers.
When an enabled voice's interrupt event occurs, the voice number is placed in this register for the processor to read.
A write to register 0x0E in any page block does nothing: the case holds only a break.
MAME's shared start and its interrupt acknowledgement both set the vector byte to 0x80, and the constructor gives the active voice count 0x1F.
